quoted_clause: the ~436 GB KV budget (640 − 140 − 64, §3(b)) supports ~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K-token requests per host before KV pressure.
observed: Uses initial 9.2K KV (24.1 GB) to estimate concurrent requests, while Ch 7's canonical concurrency uses max 9.5K KV (24.9 GB) and gives 17.51, floor 17.
correction: Either change to '~436/24.9 ≈ 17.5, floor 17' or add 'initial prefill-only; end-of-generation capacity is 17'.
acceptance_test: Ch 5 mini-case concurrency matches Ch 7 canonical floor 17 for full request lifetime, or explicitly distinguishes initial vs max KV.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05/chapter-05.md §8 reads 'the ~436 GB KV budget (640 − 140 − 64, §3(b)) supports ~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K-token requests per host before KV pressure' (436/24.1 = 18.09), while the canonical concurrency everywhere else is sized at the 9.5K end-of-generation KV: 436/24.9 = 17.5, floor 17 (ch7:27/123, ch17 Table 17-1, ch18:105 use C = 17).
fix_instruction: In the Ch 5 §8 mini-case change to '~436/24.9 ≈ 17.5, i.e. 17 whole-slot concurrent 9,500-token requests per host (Ch 17); against the 9.2K initial KV alone the quotient is 18.1' so the number matches the canonical floor of 17.

quoted_clause: MoE total parameters exceed the dense 70B
observed: The claim is phrased as a general property of MoE models. Not all MoE models have more than 70B total parameters — e.g., Mixtral 8x7B has ~47B total (8 experts × ~7B, with ~13B active per token), which is less than 70B. A reader could generalize this to 'all MoE models are bigger than 70B' and incorrectly reject viable MoE options.
correction: Qualify: 'the MoE challenger's total parameters exceed the dense 70B' or 'a 70B-class MoE's total parameters exceed the dense 70B, so the 140 GB weight floor grows.'
acceptance_test: The corrected sentence cannot be read as a universal claim about all MoE models; a counterexample (Mixtral 8x7B at ~47B total) no longer contradicts it.
verdict_evidence: ch5 L195 'the MoE challenger from Ch 3 was rejected on total-weight residency and compute grounds: MoE total parameters exceed the dense 70B' contradicts ch3 L178, where the challenger is 47B total/12.8B active with ~94 GB resident ('a drop of 46 GB, ~32.9%' below 140 GB) and is explicitly not rejected: 'The team therefore does not select the challenger yet ... remain unresolved [UNRESOLVED].'
fix_instruction: Rewrite the parenthetical to match Ch 3: the ~47B/12.8B-active challenger was not rejected on residency (94 GB resident < 140 GB dense); the dense 70B stands only as the provisional choice because equal-task quality, placement and measured goodput remain [UNRESOLVED], with expert dispatch/placement as the added cost. Do not assert that MoE total parameters exceed the dense 70B, and do not infer per-token compute from total parameters.

quoted_clause: [canonical scenario][DERIVED] KV cache cost per token at FP16: for a Llama‑style 70B model, n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, bytes per element = 2 (FP16). KV cache per token = n_layers × 2 × d_model × bytes = 80 ×2 × 8192 ×2 = 2,621,440 bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token
observed: The arithmetic is a full-MHA computation (K and V each at d_model = 8192), but it is attributed to a 'Llama-style 70B model'. Every widely deployed Llama-2/Llama-3 70B uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads of head_dim 128, i.e. n_kv_dim = 1024, not 8192. For such a model the KV footprint per token is 80 × 2 × 1024 × 2 = 327,680 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB/token — 8× smaller than the figure printed here. The book's canonical KV figure is (correctly, per house convention) the full-MHA reference; the defect is the model attribution, which invites the reader to believe a real Llama-70B deployment needs 24.1 GB of KV per 9.2K request.
correction: Rename the reference explicitly, e.g. 'for the canonical full-MHA 70B reference (n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, no GQA — the constructed teaching geometry of Ch 4 Table 4-2)', and add one sentence noting that a real Llama-2/3 70B uses GQA with 8 KV heads and therefore has ~0.33 MB/token at FP16, i.e. ~8× less KV — which is exactly the GQA effect the book teaches elsewhere. Keep the 2.62 MB/token canonical value unchanged so downstream chapters stay consistent.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 5 attributes the 2.62 MB/token full-MHA figure to a real Llama checkpoint; the text states the full-MHA assumption explicitly and states the GQA-8 alternative with its 8× factor.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:92: 'for a Llama-style 70B model, n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192 ... KV cache per token = n_layers × 2 × d_model × bytes = 2,621,440 bytes' — this sets KV width = hidden width (full MHA), but chapter-07:88 records 'LLaMA-2 70B ... has 64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads', i.e. 2×80×1024×2 = 327,680 B ≈ 0.33 MB/token, 8× less.
fix_instruction: At chapter-05:92 replace 'for a Llama-style 70B model' with 'for the canonical full-MHA 70B reference (80 layers, hidden 8192, no GQA — Ch 4 Table 4-2)' and add one clause noting a real Llama-2/3 70B is GQA-8 at ~0.33 MB/token; keep 2.62 MB/token as the canonical value.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload'
quoted_clause: the bge‑large‑en option is not justified at this scale: its quality gain over all‑mpnet‑base‑v2 is not quantified for this model pair (the table gives use cases, not metrics), and an unquantified gain would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar (≈43 vs ≈14 GFLOPs per 64‑token embedding in the table above, the same ratio as their parameter counts) — validate the gain on the target corpus before paying it.
observed: The chapter applies a decision rule to bge-large that it does not apply to the recommendation it actually makes. bge-large is rejected because its quality gain over mpnet is unquantified and would have to clear a ~3× FLOP bar. The identical argument applies to the recommended mpnet over MiniLM: the quality gain is equally unquantified for that pair, and the bar is ~4.8× FLOP (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP), which is larger. The chapter nevertheless recommends mpnet, on the strength of a 'few to ~15% MAP' prior that is explicitly labeled an unverified hypothesis and is not tied to this model pair. The recommendation therefore rests on a weaker evidential basis than the one used to reject the alternative, and the stated criterion is applied asymmetrically.
correction: Apply the bar symmetrically. Either (a) state the recommendation as a provisional shortlist entry explicitly conditional on a measured ΔMAP ≥ the stated threshold (with the threshold written as a MAP-per-FLOPS or MAP-per-storage figure so the reader can compute it), or (b) present the three candidates as a shortlist with the decision deferred to the §7 validation, and remove the word 'recommended' from Table 5-2's 'Selection status' row in favor of 'provisional shortlist, pending target-corpus validation'. If the recommendation is retained, the text must say why the ~4.8× bar is cleared while the ~3× bar is not.
acceptance_test: The same evidential standard (measured or explicitly hypothesized pair-specific quality gain vs. a stated FLOP/storage bar) is applied to every candidate in Table 5-1, including the recommended one; the recommendation's justification is either a measurement or an explicitly stated assumption that is flagged as load-bearing.
verdict_evidence: ch5 L59 scopes the prior to 'within a given embedding family or a controlled dimensionality experiment ... reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference', yet L67 makes that prior the hinge for the cross-model mpnet(110M, 14.08 GFLOP)-vs-MiniLM(23M, 2.94 GFLOP) 4.8× decision, and L69 concedes it is 'not quantified for this model pair'.
fix_instruction: At L67 mark the ~15% as a dimension/within-family upper bound that cannot be assumed to transfer across model families, and state that the mpnet-vs-MiniLM quality gap must be measured on the target corpus before the ~4.8× FLOP cost is paid.

quoted_clause: reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower storage and compute — e.g. a 384‑dim variant of the same model family can halve the index storage of a 768‑dim one (the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged, since only the final projection shrinks)
observed: The paragraph's headline claims a compute saving from reducing dimension, then states in the same sentence that the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged. The two statements are only reconcilable if 'reducing dimension' means post-hoc truncation or Matryoshka-style training of one model at multiple output widths — in which case there is no compute saving at all, only a storage saving. The compute saving the chapter actually quantifies later (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP) comes from choosing a smaller model (MiniLM vs mpnet), which is a model-size change, not a dimension change. The paragraph conflates the two, and the parenthetical 'only the final projection shrinks' describes truncation, not a trained 384-dim variant, which would have a smaller encoder.
correction: Split the claim into two: (i) truncating or Matryoshka-training a fixed encoder to a lower output width reduces index storage and query-time projection cost but leaves encoder compute essentially unchanged; (ii) substituting a smaller encoder reduces both storage and compute, and is a model-selection decision, not a dimension decision. Then state which of the two the ~4.8× FLOP figure belongs to.
acceptance_test: The §3(a) dimension paragraph and the Table 5-1 footnote use the same distinction, and the 4.8× FLOP figure is attributed to model size rather than to output dimension.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:59 promises 'lower storage and compute' in the same sentence whose parenthetical says 'the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged, since only the final projection shrinks' — two different interventions under one word; line 63 later separates them correctly ('a cross-model difference, not a dim-only sweep').
fix_instruction: At chapter-05:59 change 'for lower storage and compute' to 'for lower index storage and query-time projection cost (the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged)', keeping the 14.08-vs-2.94 GFLOP gap attributed to model size as at line 63.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) first [HYPOTHESIS] paragraph and §3(a) 'The decision hinges on...'
quoted_clause: Any observed quality‑vs‑dimension relationship (reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference) is domain‑ and corpus‑specific and must be validated on the target corpus.
observed: A quantitative empirical range ('a few to ~15% MAP') is asserted with no citation, and it is then used twice as the load-bearing quality prior for the chapter's recommendation ('the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain'). The [HYPOTHESIS] label correctly marks it as unverified, but the book elsewhere distinguishes 'unverified because no measurement exists' from 'unverified because the measurement has not been done yet'; here published reports are said to exist ('reports range from...') yet none is cited, so the reader cannot check the range, its metric definition (MAP@10? MAP over what corpus?), or its direction. The same range is restated as 'an unverified prior of a few to ~15% MAP [HYPOTHESIS]' in the takeaway, where it becomes the justification for the recommendation.
correction: Either cite the specific studies behind the range (with metric definition, corpus, and year) and scope the claim to them, or restate the range as an explicit scenario assumption with no claim that published reports exist — e.g. 'assume a quality uplift of up to 15% MAP for the larger model; this is a scenario input, not a measurement'. Then make the recommendation's dependence on that input explicit.
acceptance_test: Every numeric quality range in Ch 5 is either footnoted to a specific source with metric and corpus, or is labeled as a scenario assumption without an implied literature.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:59 asserts 'Any observed quality-vs-dimension relationship (reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference)' with no footnote or citation, and chapter-05:67 makes the top of that range load-bearing ('the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain'); the [HYPOTHESIS] tag records status but does not source the reports it invokes.
fix_instruction: Either cite the studies behind 'a few to ~15% MAP' (metric definition, corpus, year) at chapter-05:59, or restate it as a scenario input ('assume up to 15% MAP') and drop the implication that published reports exist; align the line-67 restatement with whichever form is chosen.

quoted_clause: | Tokens per dollar (generation, runtime) | 9,000 tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |
observed: The table's row label does not say which tokens are counted. The derivation shows it is output tokens only, at a single-stream rate. Two other tokens-per-dollar figures appear in the same chapter (≈242,000 and ≈285,000 tokens/$ on a combined prefill+decode basis), so a reader comparing Table 5-2 with §3(b) sees an apparent 26–32× discrepancy that is a metric-basis difference, not a finding. The table is the most likely place a reader will copy a number from.
correction: Rename the row to 'Output tokens per dollar (single-stream, 50 tok/s)' and, if a combined figure is wanted, add a second row 'Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, stated concurrency)' with its own derivation cell. Keep the two rows adjacent so the basis difference is visible at a glance.
acceptance_test: Every tokens-per-dollar figure in Ch 5 states, in the same place it appears, whether it counts output tokens or all tokens and at what concurrency; no two such figures in the chapter can be compared without reading their basis.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:79 row: '| Tokens per dollar (generation, runtime) | 9,000 tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr |' — no output-vs-total token qualifier — while chapter-05:102 prints combined-basis 285,000 and 242,000 tokens/$; the copyable cell states only that a rate times hours was divided by cost.
fix_instruction: Rename the Table 5-2 row to 'Output tokens per dollar (single-stream decode, 50 tok/s)' and, if a combined figure is wanted, add an adjacent row 'Total tokens per dollar (prefill + decode, stated concurrency)' with its own derivation cell.

page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a) paragraph beginning 'On that basis the incremental cost stays well within...'
quoted_clause: single‑core encoding fits only above ~92.5 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s)
observed: 11.14 ÷ 0.12 = 92.83, not 92.5. The 92.5 value corresponds to the rounded 11.1 GFLOP input used earlier in the same paragraph, while the parenthetical shows the unrounded 11.14. The discrepancy is immaterial to the conclusion but the printed arithmetic does not reproduce.

acceptance_test: The stated threshold reproduces from the numbers printed in the same sentence.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:65 prints '~92.5 GFLOP/s sustained per core (11.14 GFLOP ÷ 0.12 s)'; computed 11.14/0.12 = 92.833, while 92.5 = 11.1/0.12 — the displayed division does not reproduce from the numbers printed in the same parenthesis.

quoted_clause: the quality claim itself is the §3(a)/§7 item still to validate ... The parametric $Q^*$ in §5.3 shows how to decide ... the break‑even is parametric (Q* of §3(c))
observed: Two incompatible section-reference conventions are used for the same targets: '§3(a)'/'§3(c)' and '§5.3(a)'/'§5.3(c)'. Chapter references are likewise mixed: 'Ch 4', 'Ch. 7', 'Chapter 3', 'Chapter 14', 'Ch 17', 'Ch 26', 'Chapter 25'. The §5.3 form is also ambiguous with the book's own '§5.3' usage in the Common Mistakes section, where '§5.3' is used for the same subsection.
correction: Adopt one convention book-wide (e.g. '§5.3(a)' for chapter-qualified subsection references and 'Ch 7' for chapters) and normalize Ch 5 accordingly.
acceptance_test: A grep of the manuscript shows one chapter-reference style and one subsection-reference style, with no mixed forms within a chapter.
verdict_evidence: Chapter 5 mixes styles in one chapter: grep shows 'Ch. 15'(1), 'Ch. 4'(2), 'Ch. 7'(1) beside 'Ch 1/2/3/4/5/17/26' (14) and 'Chapter N' (12), plus both '§3(a)'(2)/'§5.3(a)'(2) for the same subsection (line 158 does define the §N.M reading, but not the Ch/Ch./Chapter split).
fix_instruction: Normalize Ch 5 to one convention (e.g. 'Ch N' for chapters and '§5.3(a)' for subsections), replacing 'Ch. 4/7/15' and the bare '§3(a)/§3(b)/§3(c)' forms, and keep the line-158 reading note consistent with it.

observed: 'Dense-retrieval-optimal' is an unqualified superlative in a table whose other columns are quantitative and sourced. It is also the exact kind of claim the chapter elsewhere refuses to make without measurement ('Dimension alone is not a cross-model quality metric'). The 'technical docs' use case is likewise unsourced.
correction: Replace the superlative with a factual, sourceable description of the model's training objective or published benchmark context, or drop the column and keep the table purely quantitative (dim, params, FLOPs), with use-case guidance moved to prose where it can be hedged.
acceptance_test: No cell in Table 5-1 contains an unsourced superlative; the table's columns are either quantitative or explicitly attributed.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:55 Table 5-1 cell reads '| bge-large-en | 1024 | ~335M | ~43 GFLOPs | Dense-retrieval-optimal, technical docs |' with no citation, while the same chapter refuses exactly that class of claim elsewhere ('Dimension alone is not a cross-model quality metric', line 59; 'no public study quantifies this domain-dependence', line 174).
fix_instruction: Replace 'Dense-retrieval-optimal, technical docs' with a sourceable description of the model's training objective or published benchmark context (or move use-case guidance into hedged prose) so Table 5-1 carries no unsourced superlative.

quoted_clause: supports ~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K‑token requests per host before KV pressure
observed: The concurrency screen divides the KV budget by the initial (prefill-only) KV footprint, but each request continues to grow its KV during decode: 300 output tokens add 300 × 2.62 MB ≈ 0.79 GB, so the steady-state footprint is ≈ 24.9 GB and the true ceiling is ≈ 17.5 requests. The figure is also a KV-only bound presented without the caveat that other limits (compute, scheduler, per-request latency) may bind first.
correction: Compute the screen at the request's maximum footprint (input + output) and state that it is a KV-only upper bound.
acceptance_test: The concurrency screen in Ch 5 uses the maximum per-request KV footprint and is labeled as a KV-only bound.
verdict_evidence: chapter-05:191 computes '~436/24.1 ≈ 18 concurrent 9.2K-token requests per host before KV pressure' on the initial prefill footprint; 436/24.1 = 18.09, but at the 9.5K max footprint the same chapter's table gives 24.9 GB (chapter-07:63), so 436/24.9 = 17.51, the value Ch 7 (:282) and Ch 17 (:25) both use.
fix_instruction: At chapter-05:191 use the 9.5K max per-request footprint (436/24.9 ≈ 17.5, conservative floor 17) and label the number a KV-only upper bound, matching Ch 7 and Ch 17.
